cards.heading: MCP extensions framework — definition
cards.question: What is the MCP extensions framework (SEP-2133) and what four structural features distinguish an extension from a core protocol capability?
cards.answer: It gives protocol capabilities a home outside the core spec: extensions carry reverse-DNS identifiers, are negotiated via an extensions capability map, live in their own delegated-maintainer repositories, and version independently.

cards.heading: Extensions Track stages
cards.question: What is the Extensions Track, and what progression does it formalize?
cards.answer: A staged maturity path for extensions, formalizing progression from experimental to official before (if ever) entering the core specification.

cards.heading: MCP Apps as official extension
cards.question: How does the MCP Apps extension let servers ship interactive UI safely?
cards.answer: Servers ship interactive HTML rendered in a sandboxed iframe; UI templates are pre-declared so hosts can prefetch and security-review them, and all UI-initiated actions travel the same JSON-RPC path (same audit/consent controls) as direct tool calls.

cards.heading: Why Tasks became an extension
cards.question: Why was Tasks pulled out of MCP core, where it shipped experimental in 2025-11-25, and reshaped as an extension?
cards.answer: Production use surfaced enough redesign need that it was rebuilt around the stateless core model: a server returns a task handle from tools/call, the client drives tasks/get/update/cancel, creation is server-directed, and tasks/list was removed because it can't be scoped safely without sessions.

cards.heading: Extensions framework — meta-lesson
cards.question: What lesson do the 2026-07-28 MCP release notes draw about how capabilities should ship going forward?
cards.answer: Extensions are now the standard way capabilities ship and stabilize before, if ever, entering the core specification.
